summary:
Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in December 2022, on the strength of a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights program. The Human Dignity Trust records the Barbados case as one of a series of constitutional challenges to colonial-era anti-gay statutes across the Eastern Caribbean.

Impunity for anti-trans violence is documented and recent enough to matter. In April 2019 a Barbadian court imposed no jail time for the violent meat-cleaver attack on Alexa Hoffmann, an outcome reported through Maurice Tomlinson and the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network. A visibly trans visitor who is assaulted should not expect a custodial sentence against the attacker.

Trans people on the island are visible and exposed at once. A second Trans Day of Remembrance vigil was held in Barbados in November 2018, organised with a national women's organisation, a local ally and veteran trans advocates, and Hoffmann has given first-person accounts of what visibility and danger look like there in daily life.

Employment offers no shield. Trans Barbadians are reported to be frequently fired or refused work for dressing in a way employers object to, and the Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill does not cover them, according to an August 2020 commentary on the island's labour rules.

The Welcome Stamp remote-work visa is marketed to outsiders on a promise of openness, while the employment regime that trans residents face gives them no protection against dismissal. Entry on that visa says nothing about how a trans worker or visitor will be treated once on the ground.
tangentialFactors:
Decriminalisation in Barbados follows the same litigation route used elsewhere in the Eastern Caribbean, so the legal direction of travel in the surrounding states is comparable; the Human Dignity Trust tracks these challenges as a group of cases rather than an isolated Barbadian reform.

The island has an organised community, with groups such as Equals and B-GLAD, a functioning state and a degree of social conservatism that is present but not dominant. Tourist areas are accustomed to a diverse range of visitors, which shapes everyday encounters differently from the environment trans residents navigate at work.

The gap between the 2022 decriminalisation and the 2019 impunity outcome in the Hoffmann attack shows that a liberalised statute and a protective enforcement record are separate questions; the legal reform did not itself establish sentencing practice for anti-trans violence.
localsOnly:
Trans Barbadians face dismissal or refusal of employment on grounds of presentation, and the Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill as reported in 2020 does not extend protection to them, leaving recourse to the employer and the labour market rather than to the statute.

The Trans Day of Remembrance vigil has been held more than once, with the 2018 edition organised alongside a national women's organisation and veteran trans advocates, giving the community a public memorial practice and a visible point of assembly.

Alexa Hoffmann's activism, including the 2018 constitutional claim and her public accounts of danger, has made her a named target; the 2019 sentencing in her attack produced no jail time, a fact local advocates carry into their own risk assessments.

Community organisations including Equals and B-GLAD operate openly, and advocacy has proceeded through the courts, with legal support drawn from the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights program.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in this inventory: whether Barbados provides legal gender recognition or allows a trans person to amend gender markers on passport, birth certificate or national ID. No source here addresses it, and the summary makes no claim either way.

Not sourced in this material: hate-crime or aggravated-offence provisions covering anti-trans violence, rules on access to sex-segregated facilities, recognition of trans marriages or partners, and any entry or immigration screening that could disclose a traveller's trans status. Each would need separate verification.

The status of the Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill is unresolved here: the inventory reports what the bill excludes, not whether it was enacted or amended after 2020, so current statutory coverage for trans workers is unconfirmed.

The account of frequent dismissals of trans workers comes from an August 2020 commentary rather than official or survey data, and no enforcement record for employment complaints is available in this inventory.

The December 2022 decriminalisation is documented through the Human Dignity Trust's case page rather than through the text of the court judgment or the state's response to it; the precise scope of the ruling is not set out here.
